  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsubsection"><a href="#S6.SS4.SSS5" title="In 6.4 Analysis and Ablations ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">6.4.5 </span>Expert Parallelism Considerations</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_section"><a href="#S7" title="In Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">7 </span>Related Work</span></a></li>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:
<br class="ltx_break">Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Ibne Farabi Shihab
</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_contribution ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Equal contribution.</span></span></span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">

</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Department of Civil, Construction and Environmental Engineering

</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">anujs@iastate.edu</span></a>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Mixture-of-Experts models rely on learned routers to assign tokens to experts, yet standard softmax gating provides no principled mechanism to control the tradeoff between sparsity and utilization. We propose Grassmannian MoE (GrMoE), a routing framework that operates on the Grassmannian manifold of subspaces, where gating weights arise from the concentration parameters of Matrix Bingham distributions. This construction yields a single, interpretable knob—the concentration matrix <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda</annotation></semantics></math>—that continuously controls routing entropy, replacing discrete top-<math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> selection with a smooth, geometrically principled sparsity mechanism. We further develop an amortized variational inference procedure for posterior routing distributions, enabling uncertainty-aware expert assignment that naturally resists expert collapse. We formally prove tight bounds relating the Bingham concentration spectrum to routing entropy, expected top-<math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> mass, and an exponential bound on expert collapse, establishing the first formal theory of concentration-controlled sparsity. On synthetic routing tasks, a 350M-parameter MoE language model with 8 experts, a 1.3B-parameter model with 16 experts, and a 2.7B-parameter model with 32 experts, GrMoE achieves 0% routing collapse across all seeds, comparable or better perplexity with 15–30% improved load balance, and a smooth monotonic relationship between concentration and effective sparsity that enables post-hoc sparsity tuning without retraining. Token-level analysis reveals that experts learn heterogeneous concentration values that correlate with linguistic specialization, providing interpretable routing behavior.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Mixture-of-Experts architectures achieve favorable scaling by activating only a subset of parameters per input <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Riquelme et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, with a learned router determining which experts process each token. Despite strong empirical results <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fedus et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lepikhin et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and successful deployment at massive scale in systems like Mixtral <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and DeepSeek-V3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI, 2024</a>)</cite>, current routing mechanisms suffer from fundamental limitations that hinder both training stability and deployment flexibility.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Standard softmax gating computes router probabilities as <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g(x)=\mathrm{softmax}(W_{r}x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>softmax</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g(x)=\mathrm{softmax}(W_{r}x)</annotation></semantics></math> and selects the top-<math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> experts. This formulation creates three persistent problems. First, expert collapse: a few experts dominate routing, leaving others undertrained and effectively wasted. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chi and others (2022)</a></cite> formally analyze this representation collapse phenomenon and show it worsens with model scale. Second, training instability: discrete top-<math id="S1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> selection introduces discontinuities that make router learning sensitive to initialization and random seeds, a problem that <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zuo and others (2022)</a></cite> address through stochastic expert selection but without fully resolving. Third, no principled sparsity control: the sharpness of the routing distribution is an emergent property of training rather than a controllable parameter, forcing practitioners to retrain separate models for different compute budgets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron and others, 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Auxiliary load balancing losses <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fedus et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and expert choice routing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2022</a>)</cite> partially address collapse and balance, but they remain engineering patches rather than principled mechanisms. They introduce additional hyperparameters whose optimal values are task dependent and interact unpredictably with other training dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We observe that the routing problem has a natural geometric structure that existing methods ignore. Each expert can be associated with a subspace in the representation space—the subspace of inputs that the expert specializes in. The router’s task then reduces to determining which expert subspace best contains each input. This is precisely the problem of classification on the Grassmannian manifold <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Gr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math>, the space of <math id="S1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional subspaces of <math id="S1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>. The key advantage of this geometric perspective is that it provides a principled mechanism for controlling sparsity: the concentration parameters of distributions on the Grassmannian directly determine how sharply the routing distribution peaks, giving us an interpretable knob that replaces the ad hoc combination of top-<math id="S1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> selection and auxiliary losses.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Building on this observation, we propose Grassmannian MoE (GrMoE), a routing framework with three components. Each expert <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math> is associated with a point <math id="S1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[U_{e}]\in\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>Gr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[U_{e}]\in\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math>, an equivalence class of orthonormal frames spanning a <math id="S1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional subspace. Routing weights arise from a Matrix Bingham distribution on <math id="S1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Gr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> whose concentration matrix <math id="S1.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda</annotation></semantics></math> provides a continuous, interpretable control over routing sparsity. An amortization network produces per-token posterior distributions over routing assignments, enabling uncertainty-aware expert selection that naturally resists collapse.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our work makes four contributions. First, we formalize the connection between MoE routing and classification on the Grassmannian, deriving a new gating mechanism from the Matrix Bingham distribution (Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Method: Grassmannian MoE Routing ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). Second, we prove rigorous bounds relating the Bingham concentration spectrum to routing entropy, expected top-<math id="S1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> mass, and collapse resistance (Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Theoretical Analysis: Concentration and Sparsity ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). Third, we develop an amortized variational inference procedure for posterior routing that is as efficient as standard gating but provides uncertainty estimates (Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Amortized Variational Routing ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>). Fourth, we demonstrate empirically that GrMoE reduces routing collapse, improves load balance, and enables post-hoc sparsity tuning on synthetic tasks, a 350M-parameter model with 8 experts, a 1.3B-parameter model with 16 experts, and a 2.7B-parameter model with 32 experts (Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Experiments ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background and Notation</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce the key concepts underlying our approach: MoE routing, the Grassmannian manifold, and the Matrix Bingham distribution.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Mixture-of-Experts Routing</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An MoE layer with <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> experts <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{f_{1},\ldots,f_{N}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{f_{1},\ldots,f_{N}\}</annotation></semantics></math> and a router <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\Delta^{N-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\Delta^{N-1}</annotation></semantics></math> computes <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{MoE}(x)=\sum_{e=1}^{N}g_{e}(x)\cdot f_{e}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>MoE</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{MoE}(x)=\sum_{e=1}^{N}g_{e}(x)\cdot f_{e}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shazeer et al., 2017</a>)</cite>. Standard top-<math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> routing selects the <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> experts with highest <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{e}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{e}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> values and zeros out the rest. The router is typically parameterized as <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g(x)=\mathrm{softmax}(W_{r}x+\text{noise})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>softmax</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mtext>noise</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g(x)=\mathrm{softmax}(W_{r}x+\text{noise})</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>, a design that has remained largely unchanged since its introduction despite advances in pre-training objectives <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al., 2020</a>)</cite> and model architectures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The fundamental limitation of this formulation is that the router operates on a single linear projection of the input. Each expert is represented by a single vector <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> (a row of <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{r}</annotation></semantics></math>), and the routing decision is based on the dot product <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{e}^{\top}x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{e}^{\top}x</annotation></semantics></math>. This means the router can only distinguish inputs based on their projection onto a one-dimensional subspace per expert. In contrast, GrMoE represents each expert by a <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional subspace, providing a much richer representation of expert specialization that can capture multi-dimensional patterns in the input space.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>The Grassmannian Manifold</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Grassmannian <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Gr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> is the set of <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional subspaces of <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>. Each point <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[U]\in\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>U</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>Gr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[U]\in\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> is an equivalence class <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[U]=\{UO:O\in O(k)\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>U</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[U]=\{UO:O\in O(k)\}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U\in V_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U\in V_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d})</annotation></semantics></math> is any orthonormal basis for the subspace. The manifold has dimension <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k(d-k)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k(d-k)</annotation></semantics></math>. The projection distance between subspaces is</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)}([U_{1}],[U_{2}])=\sqrt{k-\|U_{1}^{\top}U_{2}\|_{F}^{2}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>Gr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)}([U_{1}],[U_{2}])=\sqrt{k-\|U_{1}^{\top}U_{2}\|_{F}^{2}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">which equals zero for identical subspaces and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sqrt{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msqrt><mi>k</mi></msqrt><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{k}</annotation></semantics></math> for orthogonal ones.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The Grassmannian is a quotient of the Stiefel manifold: <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)=V_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d})/O(k)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>Gr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)=V_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d})/O(k)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(k)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(k)</annotation></semantics></math> is the orthogonal group acting by right multiplication. This means that any two orthonormal bases <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="UO" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">UO</annotation></semantics></math> (for <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O\in O(k)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O\in O(k)</annotation></semantics></math>) represent the same subspace. In our implementation, we work with representative frames <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{e}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{e}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d})</annotation></semantics></math> and ensure that all computations are invariant to the choice of representative. The subspace affinity <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|P_{e}x\|^{2}=\|U_{e}^{\top}x\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|P_{e}x\|^{2}=\|U_{e}^{\top}x\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is automatically invariant since <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|U_{e}O^{\top}x\|^{2}=\|U_{e}^{\top}x\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>O</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|U_{e}O^{\top}x\|^{2}=\|U_{e}^{\top}x\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> for any <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O\in O(k)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O\in O(k)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The projection distance (Eq. <a href="#S2.E1" title="In 2.2 The Grassmannian Manifold ‣ 2 Background and Notation ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) is one of several natural metrics on the Grassmannian. We use it because it has a simple closed form and is directly related to the subspace affinity that appears in our gating mechanism. Other metrics, such as the geodesic distance (based on principal angles) or the chordal distance, would yield equivalent routing behavior up to a monotone transformation of the affinities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>The Matrix Bingham Distribution</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Matrix Bingham distribution on <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Gr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math> has density with respect to the uniform measure <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chikuse, 2003</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoff, 2009</a>)</cite>:</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p([U]\mid\Lambda,M)=\frac{1}{Z(\Lambda)}\exp\!\big(\mathrm{tr}(\Lambda M^{\top}UU^{\top}M)\big)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>U</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mi>tr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p([U]\mid\Lambda,M)=\frac{1}{Z(\Lambda)}\exp\!\big(\mathrm{tr}(\Lambda M^{\top}UU^{\top}M)\big)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>diag</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d})</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo rspace="0.1389em">≥</mo><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.1389em">⋯</mo><mo lspace="0.1389em">≥</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{d}</annotation></semantics></math> is the concentration matrix, <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\in O(d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\in O(d)</annotation></semantics></math> is the modal orientation, and <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z(\Lambda)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z(\Lambda)</annotation></semantics></math> is the normalizing constant. The concentration parameters <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> control how peaked the distribution is around the modal subspace spanned by the first <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> columns of <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>. When <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{k+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{k+1}</annotation></semantics></math> is large, the distribution concentrates sharply; when all <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are equal, it reduces to the uniform distribution on <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Gr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math>. This gives us exactly the knob we need: the spectral gap of <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda</annotation></semantics></math> controls sparsity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To build intuition, consider the extreme cases. When all <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are equal, the Bingham distribution is uniform on <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Gr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Gr}(k,d)</annotation></semantics></math>, and every subspace is equally likely—this corresponds to completely diffuse routing where no expert is preferred. When <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{1}=\cdots=\lambda_{k}\gg\lambda_{k+1}=\cdots=\lambda_{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.1389em">⋯</mo><mo lspace="0.1389em">=</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>≫</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.1389em">⋯</mo><mo lspace="0.1389em">=</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{1}=\cdots=\lambda_{k}\gg\lambda_{k+1}=\cdots=\lambda_{d}</annotation></semantics></math>, the distribution concentrates sharply on the modal subspace, corresponding to hard routing where a single expert dominates. Between these extremes, the spectral gap <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{k}-\lambda_{k+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{k}-\lambda_{k+1}</annotation></semantics></math> interpolates smoothly, providing a continuous control over routing sharpness. This is fundamentally different from the discrete jump between top-1 and top-2 routing in standard MoE architectures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The normalizing constant <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z(\Lambda)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z(\Lambda)</annotation></semantics></math> does not have a closed form, which is a common challenge with distributions on manifolds. We provide the saddle-point approximation formula of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kume and Wood (2005)</a></cite> in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Bingham Normalizing Constant Approximation ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> and validate its accuracy empirically in Section <a href="#S6.SS4.SSS4" title="6.4.4 Bingham Normalizer Validation ‣ 6.4 Analysis and Ablations ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.4.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method: Grassmannian MoE Routing</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now describe the three components of GrMoE: subspace representations for experts, Bingham concentration gating, and continuous sparsity control.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Expert Subspace Representation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We represent each expert <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e\in\{1,\ldots,N\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e\in\{1,\ldots,N\}</annotation></semantics></math> by a learnable subspace <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[U_{e}]\in\mathrm{Gr}(k_{r},d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>Gr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[U_{e}]\in\mathrm{Gr}(k_{r},d)</annotation></semantics></math>, parameterized by an orthonormal frame <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{e}\in V_{k_{r}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{e}\in V_{k_{r}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> is the routing rank (a hyperparameter, typically <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}\approx d/N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}\approx d/N</annotation></semantics></math>). The projection operator for expert <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{e}=U_{e}U_{e}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{e}=U_{e}U_{e}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Note that we never explicitly form the <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\times d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\times d</annotation></semantics></math> projection matrix <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{e}</annotation></semantics></math>. Instead, the subspace affinity <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|P_{e}x\|^{2}=\|U_{e}^{\top}x\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|P_{e}x\|^{2}=\|U_{e}^{\top}x\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is computed efficiently as a matrix-vector product <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{e}^{\top}x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{e}^{\top}x</annotation></semantics></math> (cost <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(dk_{r})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(dk_{r})</annotation></semantics></math>) followed by a squared norm (cost <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(k_{r})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(k_{r})</annotation></semantics></math>), for a total cost of <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(dk_{r})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(dk_{r})</annotation></semantics></math> per expert per token. With <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> experts, the total routing cost is <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(Ndk_{r})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(Ndk_{r})</annotation></semantics></math>, compared to <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(Nd)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(Nd)</annotation></semantics></math> for standard softmax gating. Because <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}\ll d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>≪</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}\ll d</annotation></semantics></math>, the routing cost remains a negligible fraction of the total forward pass cost (see Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Experiments ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> for timing breakdowns).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Bingham Concentration Gating</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a token representation <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>, we define the routing affinity of expert <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math> via the Grassmannian inner product <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{e}(x)=\|P_{e}x\|^{2}=x^{\top}U_{e}U_{e}^{\top}x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{e}(x)=\|P_{e}x\|^{2}=x^{\top}U_{e}U_{e}^{\top}x</annotation></semantics></math>, which measures how much of <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>’s energy lies in expert <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>’s subspace. Rather than applying a standard softmax with temperature, we derive a principled gating mechanism from the Bingham distribution. We define a token-conditioned Bingham distribution over the discrete expert index <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{e}(x;\Lambda)=\frac{\exp\!\big(\mathrm{tr}(\Lambda_{e}P_{e}xx^{\top})\big)}{\sum_{e^{\prime}}\exp\!\big(\mathrm{tr}(\Lambda_{e^{\prime}}P_{e^{\prime}}xx^{\top})\big)}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mi>tr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mi>tr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{e}(x;\Lambda)=\frac{\exp\!\big(\mathrm{tr}(\Lambda_{e}P_{e}xx^{\top})\big)}{\sum_{e^{\prime}}\exp\!\big(\mathrm{tr}(\Lambda_{e^{\prime}}P_{e^{\prime}}xx^{\top})\big)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where each expert has its own concentration matrix <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> (or, in the simplified version, a scalar concentration <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{e}</annotation></semantics></math>). In the scalar case where <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda_{e}=\kappa_{e}I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda_{e}=\kappa_{e}I</annotation></semantics></math>, this simplifies to</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{e}(x;\kappa)=\frac{\exp\!\big(\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}\big)}{\sum_{e^{\prime}}\exp\!\big(\kappa_{e^{\prime}}\|P_{e^{\prime}}x\|^{2}\big)}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>κ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{e}(x;\kappa)=\frac{\exp\!\big(\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}\big)}{\sum_{e^{\prime}}\exp\!\big(\kappa_{e^{\prime}}\|P_{e^{\prime}}x\|^{2}\big)}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">The concentration parameters <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> are learned per expert, but crucially, they also serve as a post-hoc sparsity control: increasing all <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> sharpens the routing distribution, while decreasing them diffuses it.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Continuous Sparsity via Concentration</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Instead of discrete top-<math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> selection, we define soft top-<math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> routing via concentration scaling:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g^{(\alpha)}_{e}(x)=\frac{\exp\!\big(\alpha\cdot\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}\big)}{\sum_{e^{\prime}}\exp\!\big(\alpha\cdot\kappa_{e^{\prime}}\|P_{e^{\prime}}x\|^{2}\big)}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g^{(\alpha)}_{e}(x)=\frac{\exp\!\big(\alpha\cdot\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}\big)}{\sum_{e^{\prime}}\exp\!\big(\alpha\cdot\kappa_{e^{\prime}}\|P_{e^{\prime}}x\|^{2}\big)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> is a global sparsity dial. At <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0</annotation></semantics></math>, routing is uniform; as <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, routing converges to hard top-1. The model is trained at <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1</annotation></semantics></math> and can be deployed at any <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> without retraining. This mechanism is categorically different from temperature scaling of softmax gating: the <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> values encode learned, per-expert sparsity preferences derived from the Bingham geometry, rather than applying uniform sharpening.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Connection to Softmax Gating</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Standard softmax gating evaluates expert affinity via a linear projection <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{e}^{\top}x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{e}^{\top}x</annotation></semantics></math>. GrMoE with <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}=1</annotation></semantics></math> (rank-1 subspaces, i.e., lines through the origin) yields an affinity of <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|P_{e}x\|^{2}=(u_{e}^{\top}x)^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|P_{e}x\|^{2}=(u_{e}^{\top}x)^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{e}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>𝕊</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{e}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}</annotation></semantics></math> is a unit vector. While softmax gating is highly sensitive to directionality (sign), GrMoE correctly respects the symmetry of subspaces, evaluating whether the token’s energy lies along the expert’s characteristic axis regardless of sign. GrMoE generalizes this geometric perspective in two directions: higher capacity representations via higher-rank subspaces (<math id="S3.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math>) and learned, non-uniform sparsity preferences via concentration (<math id="S3.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{e}\neq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>≠</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{e}\neq 1</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This connection also clarifies why GrMoE’s post-hoc sparsity control (via <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>) is fundamentally different from temperature scaling of softmax gating. In the softmax case, temperature scaling uniformly sharpens or softens all routing decisions, regardless of the underlying structure. In GrMoE, the <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> values encode learned, per-expert sparsity preferences that reflect the Bingham geometry of each expert’s specialization. Scaling by <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> preserves these relative preferences while globally adjusting the sparsity level, yielding a smooth and predictable control that temperature scaling cannot match (as we demonstrate empirically in Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Experiments ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Theoretical Analysis: Concentration and Sparsity</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now establish formal connections between the Bingham concentration spectrum and key routing properties. These results provide the theoretical foundation for concentration-controlled sparsity and collapse resistance. All corresponding proofs are detailed in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Proofs ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 1</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Concentration–Entropy Bound)<span id="Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g^{(\alpha)}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g^{(\alpha)}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> be the GrMoE routing distribution (Eq. <a href="#S3.E5" title="In 3.3 Continuous Sparsity via Concentration ‣ 3 Method: Grassmannian MoE Routing ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) with <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> experts. Let <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="H(\alpha,x)=-\sum_{e}g_{e}^{(\alpha)}(x)\log g_{e}^{(\alpha)}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.055em">−</mo><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>e</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>log</mi><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H(\alpha,x)=-\sum_{e}g_{e}^{(\alpha)}(x)\log g_{e}^{(\alpha)}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> be the routing entropy for token <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>. Then <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H(\alpha,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H(\alpha,x)</annotation></semantics></math> is strictly bounded by the concentration gap <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{\kappa}(x)=\max_{e}\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{e}\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>κ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>e</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{\kappa}(x)=\max_{e}\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{e}\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span></p>
<table id="S4.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H(\alpha,x)\geq\log N-\alpha\cdot\Delta_{\kappa}(x)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>κ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H(\alpha,x)\geq\log N-\alpha\cdot\Delta_{\kappa}(x).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Furthermore, the entropy reduction is exactly bounded from above globally by the concentration variance <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Gamma_{\kappa}(x)=\mathrm{Var}_{e\sim U}[\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>κ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Var</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Gamma_{\kappa}(x)=\mathrm{Var}_{e\sim U}[\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}]</annotation></semantics></math> over the uniform distribution <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math>:</span></p>
<table id="S4.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E7.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="H(\alpha,x)\leq\log N-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}\cdot\Gamma_{\kappa}(x)\cdot e^{-\alpha\cdot\delta_{\kappa}(x)}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>log</mi><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>κ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>δ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>κ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H(\alpha,x)\leq\log N-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}\cdot\Gamma_{\kappa}(x)\cdot e^{-\alpha\cdot\delta_{\kappa}(x)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Thmtheorem1.p1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{\kappa}(x)=\max_{e}\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}-\min_{e}\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>κ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>min</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{\kappa}(x)=\max_{e}\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}-\min_{e}\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is the concentration range.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This theorem has a direct practical implication: the variance of the concentration parameters <math id="S4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{e}</annotation></semantics></math>, together with the subspace affinities, strictly determines the achievable range of routing entropy.
