By learning <math id="S4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{e}</annotation></semantics></math>, GrMoE natively learns the entropy bounds for its routing regime, not just the entropy operating point.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmcorollary1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_corollary">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmcorollary1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Corollary 1</span></span><span id="Thmcorollary1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Top-<math id="Thmcorollary1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> Mass Control)<span id="Thmcorollary1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmcorollary1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmcorollary1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmcorollary1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{k}^{(\alpha)}(x)=\sum_{e\in\text{top-}k(x)}g_{e}^{(\alpha)}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>G</mi><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">top-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{k}^{(\alpha)}(x)=\sum_{e\in\text{top-}k(x)}g_{e}^{(\alpha)}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> be the mass assigned to the top-<math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> experts. Then</span></p>
<table id="S4.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E8.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="G_{k}^{(\alpha)}(x)\geq 1-(N-k)\exp\!\big(-\alpha\cdot\delta_{k}(x)\big)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>G</mi><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi><mo rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{k}^{(\alpha)}(x)\geq 1-(N-k)\exp\!\big(-\alpha\cdot\delta_{k}(x)\big)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Thmcorollary1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmcorollary1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{k}(x)=\kappa_{(k)}\|P_{(k)}x\|^{2}-\kappa_{(k+1)}\|P_{(k+1)}x\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{k}(x)=\kappa_{(k)}\|P_{(k)}x\|^{2}-\kappa_{(k+1)}\|P_{(k+1)}x\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is the <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-th concentration gap (experts sorted descendingly by their concentrated affinity <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>).</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The top-<math id="S4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> mass is exponentially controlled by the concentration gap at the <math id="S4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-th expert, providing a principled, mathematically continuous alternative to hard top-<math id="S4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> thresholding.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 2</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Collapse Resistance via Subspace Separation)<span id="Thmtheorem2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{g}_{e}=\mathbb{E}_{x}[g_{e}^{(\alpha)}(x)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{g}_{e}=\mathbb{E}_{x}[g_{e}^{(\alpha)}(x)]</annotation></semantics></math> be the expected load on expert <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>. Assume inputs <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> are drawn from a uniform mixture over experts <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\sim\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{D}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\sim\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{D}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, where for <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\sim\mathcal{D}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\sim\mathcal{D}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, the target subspace affinity satisfies <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|P_{i}x\|^{2}\geq\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>≥</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|P_{i}x\|^{2}\geq\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>, and other subspaces satisfy <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|P_{j}x\|^{2}\leq\rho\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|P_{j}x\|^{2}\leq\rho\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j\neq i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j\neq i</annotation></semantics></math> (bounded overlap limit). Let <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{\min}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{\min}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math> be the minimum and maximum expert concentrations. If the concentration-adjusted separation gap satisfies <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\equiv\gamma(\kappa_{\min}-\rho\kappa_{\max})&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>≡</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\equiv\gamma(\kappa_{\min}-\rho\kappa_{\max})&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, then the load balance coefficient of variation (<math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{CV}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>CV</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{CV}</annotation></semantics></math>) rigorously satisfies an exponential bound:</span></p>
<table id="S4.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E9.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathrm{CV}(\bar{g})\leq(N-1)\exp\!\big(-\alpha\cdot\Delta\big)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>CV</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{CV}(\bar{g})\leq(N-1)\exp\!\big(-\alpha\cdot\Delta\big).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The practical significance of this theorem is profound: it replaces the empirical observation that “load balancing losses help” with a formal structural mechanism. Since well-separated subspaces minimize geometric overlap <math id="S4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> and maximize <math id="S4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math>, geometrically controlling subspace overlap exponentially suppresses collapse (via the rigorous CV bound). This formally proves why GrMoE can dispense with standard auxiliary load balancing losses entirely.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Amortized Variational Routing</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now extend GrMoE with a variational framework that maintains a posterior distribution over expert assignments, enabling uncertainty-aware routing.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Routing as Exact Bayesian Inference</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We treat expert assignment <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\in\{1,\ldots,N\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\in\{1,\ldots,N\}</annotation></semantics></math> as a latent variable. Assuming a generative model for token representations, the exact Bingham likelihood incorporates its normalization constant: <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x\mid z=e)=\frac{1}{Z(\kappa_{e})}\exp(\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x\mid z=e)=\frac{1}{Z(\kappa_{e})}\exp(\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2})</annotation></semantics></math>. If we place a <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">capacity-aware prior</span> over experts <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(z=e)\propto Z(\kappa_{e})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∝</mo><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(z=e)\propto Z(\kappa_{e})</annotation></semantics></math>, which naturally favors experts with broader geometric tuning (lower concentration), applying Bayes’ rule precisely cancels the complex normalizers, yielding the exact posterior <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(z=e\mid x)=g_{e}(x;\kappa)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>κ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(z=e\mid x)=g_{e}(x;\kappa)</annotation></semantics></math>, which matches the GrMoE gating (Eq. <a href="#S3.E4" title="In 3.2 Bingham Concentration Gating ‣ 3 Method: Grassmannian MoE Routing ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). This reveals that GrMoE gating inherently acts as a rigorous Bayesian posterior computation without requiring complex runtime estimations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Amortized Posterior with Learned Uncertainty</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The basic posterior <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(z\mid x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(z\mid x)</annotation></semantics></math> uses the same concentration <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> for all tokens. To allow the model to express varying confidence across tokens, we introduce an amortization network <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\phi}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{N}_{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>N</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\phi}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{N}_{+}</annotation></semantics></math> that produces token-specific concentration scaling:</p>
<table id="S5.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\phi}(z=e\mid x)=\frac{\exp\!\big(h_{\phi}(x)_{e}\cdot\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}\big)}{\sum_{e^{\prime}}\exp\!\big(h_{\phi}(x)_{e^{\prime}}\cdot\kappa_{e^{\prime}}\|P_{e^{\prime}}x\|^{2}\big)}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\phi}(z=e\mid x)=\frac{\exp\!\big(h_{\phi}(x)_{e}\cdot\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}\big)}{\sum_{e^{\prime}}\exp\!\big(h_{\phi}(x)_{e^{\prime}}\cdot\kappa_{e^{\prime}}\|P_{e^{\prime}}x\|^{2}\big)}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">When <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\phi}(x)=\mathbf{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟏</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\phi}(x)=\mathbf{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, this reduces to basic GrMoE. When <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\phi}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\phi}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> varies across tokens, the model can express high confidence for tokens that clearly belong to one expert and low confidence for ambiguous tokens. The amortization network is a lightweight two-layer MLP with <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\phi}(x)=\mathrm{softmax}(\text{MLP}(x))\cdot N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>softmax</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>MLP</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\phi}(x)=\mathrm{softmax}(\text{MLP}(x))\cdot N</annotation></semantics></math>, ensuring <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{e}h_{\phi}(x)_{e}=N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>e</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{e}h_{\phi}(x)_{e}=N</annotation></semantics></math> so that average concentration is preserved. This adds fewer than 0.5% parameters to the router.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The design of the amortization network deserves comment. We normalize the output via <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{softmax}(\cdot)\cdot N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>softmax</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{softmax}(\cdot)\cdot N</annotation></semantics></math> rather than using a ReLU or exponential activation because the normalization constraint <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{e}h_{\phi}(x)_{e}=N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>e</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{e}h_{\phi}(x)_{e}=N</annotation></semantics></math> ensures that the average concentration across experts is preserved for every token. Without this constraint, the amortization network could learn to uniformly increase or decrease all concentrations, which would be equivalent to changing <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> and would interfere with the post-hoc sparsity control. The <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{softmax}\cdot N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>softmax</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{softmax}\cdot N</annotation></semantics></math> normalization decouples the amortization network’s role (redistributing concentration across experts for a given token) from the global sparsity dial <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> (uniformly scaling all concentrations).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We also considered a more expressive amortization architecture that produces a full <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N\times N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N\times N</annotation></semantics></math> concentration matrix per token, but found that the additional expressiveness did not improve PPL and increased routing overhead by 3%. The scalar per-expert scaling is sufficient because the subspace affinities <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|P_{e}x\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|P_{e}x\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> already capture the geometric relationship between the token and each expert; the amortization network only needs to modulate the confidence of these geometric measurements, not replace them.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Training Objective</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train GrMoE with the standard MoE language modeling loss plus a principled geometric constraint that fulfills the requirements of Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2 (Collapse Resistance via Subspace Separation). ‣ 4 Theoretical Analysis: Concentration and Sparsity ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>:</p>
<table id="S5.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S5.E11"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S5.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S5.E11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}}+\beta\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{subspace}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>LM</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>subspace</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}}+\beta\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{subspace}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S5.E12"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S5.E12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{subspace}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>subspace</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{subspace}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S5.E12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\sum_{e\neq e^{\prime}}\max\!\big(0,\|U_{e}^{\top}U_{e^{\prime}}\|_{F}^{2}-\rho_{0}k_{r}\big)." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>≠</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow></munder></mstyle><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.808em;" width="1.808em"><mi>max</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\sum_{e\neq e^{\prime}}\max\!\big(0,\|U_{e}^{\top}U_{e^{\prime}}\|_{F}^{2}-\rho_{0}k_{r}\big).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The subspace regularizer encourages expert subspaces to be well separated (overlap tightly bounded below <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{0}k_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{0}k_{r}</annotation></semantics></math>), which directly bounds the collapse misrouting rate and exponentially controls load balance. This replaces the standard load balancing loss with a geometrically motivated alternative: experts should specialize in different orthogonal directions of the representation space. The expert subspace parameters <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> are optimized on the Stiefel manifold using Riemannian Adam <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bécigneul and Ganea, 2019</a>)</cite>, while all other parameters are optimized with standard Adam.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The choice to optimize <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> on the Stiefel manifold (rather than using an unconstrained parameterization followed by projection) is important for two reasons. First, it ensures that the expert frames remain exactly orthonormal throughout training, so the subspace affinities <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|P_{e}x\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|P_{e}x\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> are always well defined and numerically stable. Second, it avoids the “projection problem” that arises when optimizing in ambient space and projecting: the projected gradient can differ significantly from the Riemannian gradient, leading to slower convergence and suboptimal solutions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For scaling to large <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>, we note that the <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(N^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(N^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> pairwise overlap computation in <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{subspace}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>subspace</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{subspace}}</annotation></semantics></math> can be replaced by sampling <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> random pairs per step. We find that <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=4N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=4N</annotation></semantics></math> suffices to match the full computation (Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Sampled-Pairs Approximation ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>), making the cost strictly linear in <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="algorithm1" class="ltx_float ltx_algorithm">
<div id="algorithm1.3" class="ltx_listing ltx_lst_numbers_left ltx_listing">
<div id="algorithm1.3.1" class="ltx_listingline">
<span id="algorithm1.3.1.1" class="ltx_text"><span id="algorithm1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input:</span> </span>Token <math id="algorithm1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>, experts <math id="algorithm1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{(U_{e},\kappa_{e},f_{e})\}_{e=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{(U_{e},\kappa_{e},f_{e})\}_{e=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math>, amortizer <math id="algorithm1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.3.2" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.3.2.1" class="ltx_text"><span id="algorithm1.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Output:</span> </span>MoE output <math id="algorithm1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.3.3" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.3.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> <em id="algorithm1.3.3.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic"><math id="algorithm1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e=1,\ldots,N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e=1,\ldots,N</annotation></semantics></math></em> <span id="algorithm1.3.3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.3.4" class="ltx_listingline"> <span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span> <math id="algorithm1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{e}\leftarrow\|U_{e}^{\top}x\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{e}\leftarrow\|U_{e}^{\top}x\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> ;  <span id="algorithm1.3.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">// </span><span id="algorithm1.3.4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Subspace affinity</span>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.3.5" class="ltx_listingline">end for
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.3.6" class="ltx_listingline"><math id="algorithm1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{h}\leftarrow h_{\phi}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝒉</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{h}\leftarrow h_{\phi}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> ;  <span id="algorithm1.3.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">// </span><span id="algorithm1.3.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Token-specific concentration</span>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.3.7" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.3.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> <em id="algorithm1.3.7.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic"><math id="algorithm1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e=1,\ldots,N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e=1,\ldots,N</annotation></semantics></math></em> <span id="algorithm1.3.7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.3.8" class="ltx_listingline"> <span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span> <math id="algorithm1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{e}\leftarrow h_{e}\cdot\kappa_{e}\cdot a_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{e}\leftarrow h_{e}\cdot\kappa_{e}\cdot a_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> ;  <span id="algorithm1.3.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">// </span><span id="algorithm1.3.8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Concentrated logits</span>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.3.9" class="ltx_listingline">end for
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.3.10" class="ltx_listingline"><math id="algorithm1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{g}\leftarrow\mathrm{softmax}(\bm{\ell})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝒈</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mi>softmax</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{g}\leftarrow\mathrm{softmax}(\bm{\ell})</annotation></semantics></math> ;  <span id="algorithm1.3.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">// </span><span id="algorithm1.3.10.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Routing weights</span>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.3.11" class="ltx_listingline"><math id="algorithm1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\leftarrow\sum_{e}g_{e}\cdot f_{e}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo rspace="0.111em" stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>e</mi></msub><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\leftarrow\sum_{e}g_{e}\cdot f_{e}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> ;  <span id="algorithm1.3.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">// </span><span id="algorithm1.3.11.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Weighted expert output</span>

</div>
</div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="algorithm1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span>GrMoE Forward Pass</figcaption>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate GrMoE on synthetic routing tasks for controlled analysis, on a 350M-parameter MoE language model for direct comparison with prior work, and on a 1.3B-parameter model with 16 experts to validate scaling behavior. Across all settings, we assess routing accuracy, load balance, collapse resistance, and the ability to tune sparsity post hoc.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the synthetic task, we construct a controlled routing problem with <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=8</annotation></semantics></math> experts and <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=128</annotation></semantics></math>. Ground truth expert subspaces are randomly generated with controlled overlap <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ρ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>. Tokens are sampled from a mixture <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\sim\sum_{e}\pi_{e}\cdot\mathcal{N}(0,P_{e}+\sigma^{2}(I-P_{e}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo rspace="0.111em">∼</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>e</mi></msub><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\sim\sum_{e}\pi_{e}\cdot\mathcal{N}(0,P_{e}+\sigma^{2}(I-P_{e}))</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> is the ground truth expert subspace projector and <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma^{2}&lt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma^{2}&lt;1</annotation></semantics></math> controls the signal-to-noise ratio. We vary <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ρ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> to create easy and hard routing scenarios.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the easy setting, we use <math id="S6.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho^{*}=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>ρ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho^{*}=0.1</annotation></semantics></math> (well-separated subspaces) and <math id="S6.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma^{2}=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma^{2}=0.1</annotation></semantics></math> (high SNR). For the hard setting, we use <math id="S6.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho^{*}=0.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>ρ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho^{*}=0.4</annotation></semantics></math> (overlapping subspaces) and <math id="S6.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma^{2}=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma^{2}=0.5</annotation></semantics></math> (low SNR). The results in Table <a href="#S6.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 6.2 Synthetic Task Results ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> report the easy setting; in the hard setting, GrMoE’s advantage grows: assignment accuracy is 78.3% (vs. 68.1% for Softmax Top-1 and 72.4% for vMF-Gate), and the collapse rate for Softmax Top-1 rises to 62% while GrMoE remains at 0%. This confirms that the Grassmannian structure is most valuable precisely when routing is difficult.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For the 350M language model, we train a 12-layer MoE Transformer on OpenWebText <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2019</a>)</cite> with <math id="S6.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=8</annotation></semantics></math> experts per MoE layer, MoE layers at every other Transformer block (6 MoE layers total), <math id="S6.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d=768" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>768</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=768</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S6.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}=48" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>48</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}=48</annotation></semantics></math>, training on 4<math id="S6.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>A100 GPUs with batch size 256 for 100K steps. For the 1.3B model, we scale to 24 layers with <math id="S6.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d=2048" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2048</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=2048</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S6.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=16</annotation></semantics></math> experts, <math id="S6.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}=64</annotation></semantics></math>, MoE at every other layer (12 MoE layers), training for 150K steps on 8<math id="S6.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>A100 GPUs. The 1.3B model uses grouped-query attention following the Mistral architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang and others, 2023</a>)</cite> to verify that GrMoE routing is compatible with modern attention variants. The subspace regularization uses sampled pairs (<math id="S6.SS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=4N=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=4N=64</annotation></semantics></math>) rather than all <math id="S6.SS1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\binom{16}{2}=120" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mn>16</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>120</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\binom{16}{2}=120</annotation></semantics></math> pairs, keeping the cost linear.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We compare against six baselines: Softmax Top-<math id="S6.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shazeer et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, Switch Transformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fedus et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, Expert Choice <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, Hash routing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Roller et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, Soft MoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Puigcerver et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and vMF-Gate (softmax gating with rank-1 hyperspherical normalization, our ablation). We report perplexity (PPL), expert load balance (CV = coefficient of variation of expert load), routing entropy <math id="S6.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math>, and collapse rate (fraction of seeds where at least one expert receives fewer than 1% of tokens).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Synthetic Task Results</h3>

<figure id="S6.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S6.T1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S6.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Synthetic routing task: recovery of ground truth expert assignments across 50 random seeds.</span></figcaption>
<table id="S6.T1.5" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S6.T1.5.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S6.T1.5.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt">Method</th>
<td id="S6.T1.5.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">Assign. Acc<math id="S6.T1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="S6.T1.5.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">CV<math id="S6.T1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td id="S6.T1.5.9.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">1.48</td></tr>

</table>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GrMoE achieves 91.7% assignment accuracy (Table <a href="#S6.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 6.2 Synthetic Task Results ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), outperforming all baselines by more than 5 points. The 0% collapse rate across all 50 seeds confirms Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2 (Collapse Resistance via Subspace Separation). ‣ 4 Theoretical Analysis: Concentration and Sparsity ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>: rigorously well-separated subspaces enforced by <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{subspace}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>subspace</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{subspace}}</annotation></semantics></math> prevent collapse inherently without arbitrary auxiliary balancing losses. Expert Choice also achieves 0% collapse but at the cost of lower assignment accuracy, since it forces balanced loads regardless of data structure. Soft MoE achieves strong accuracy but still collapses in 8% of seeds, showing that its soft token mixing does not fully resolve the stability problem.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Varying <math id="S6.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> at inference time produces a smooth, monotonic decrease in routing entropy (Figure <a href="#S6.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 6.2 Synthetic Task Results ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). This validates Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1 (Concentration–Entropy Bound). ‣ 4 Theoretical Analysis: Concentration and Sparsity ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>: the concentration variance <math id="S6.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Gamma_{\kappa}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>κ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Gamma_{\kappa}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> strictly bounds and shapes the entropy trajectory exactly as mathematically predicted. By contrast, temperature scaling of softmax gating produces erratic, non-monotonic entropy trajectories for some seeds, because the softmax logits do not have the structured relationship to sparsity that the Bingham concentration parameters provide. This difference is not merely aesthetic: it means that GrMoE’s sparsity behavior is predictable from the learned parameters, while softmax temperature scaling requires empirical calibration for each deployment scenario.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17798v1/fig2_concentration_sparsity.svg" id="S6.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/185;" width="476" height="185"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S6.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Post-hoc sparsity control via concentration scaling. GrMoE provides smooth, predictable sparsity control, whereas softmax temperature scaling does not.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>

</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">On the 350M model (Table <a href="#S6.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 6.3 Language Model Results ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, top), GrMoE with amortization achieves the best perplexity (18.1) while maintaining a 0% collapse rate and strong load balance. The key comparison is against vMF-Gate, which uses directional statistics but not subspace structure: GrMoE’s 0.4-point PPL improvement and dramatically better stability (0% vs. 20% collapse) demonstrate the mathematical value of subspace routing over rank-1 directional routing. Soft MoE achieves competitive PPL (18.4) but still collapses in 10% of seeds and has worse load balance (CV .112 vs. .074).</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The 1.3B model with 16 experts (Table <a href="#S6.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 6.3 Language Model Results ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, middle) validates that GrMoE scales beyond the small-model regime. The collapse problem worsens at larger <math id="S6.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> for baselines—Softmax Top-2 collapses in 55% of seeds with 16 experts vs. 40% with 8—while GrMoE maintains 0% collapse.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To push further into the regime where routing quality is critical, we train a 2.7B model with <math id="S6.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=32</annotation></semantics></math> experts (Table <a href="#S6.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 6.3 Language Model Results ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, bottom), matching the scale of recent open MoE models like OLMoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Muennighoff et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. At <math id="S6.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=32</annotation></semantics></math>, the collapse problem becomes severe for baselines: Softmax Top-2 collapses in 65% of seeds, and even Soft MoE collapses in 20%. GrMoE maintains 0% collapse with strong load balance (CV .092) and achieves the best PPL (11.5). The sampled-pairs approximation to <math id="S6.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{subspace}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>subspace</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{subspace}}</annotation></semantics></math> uses <math id="S6.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=128</annotation></semantics></math> pairs (vs. <math id="S6.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\binom{32}{2}=496" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mn>32</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>496</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\binom{32}{2}=496</annotation></semantics></math> full pairs), keeping the regularization cost linear while introducing no measurable degradation (CV .092 vs. .090 with full computation on a subset of steps).</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">GrMoE’s standard deviation across seeds is 0.2 at all three scales, matching Expert Choice and substantially lower than the 0.3–0.4 observed for softmax-based methods. This reduced variance translates to more reliable training when compute budgets are tight. All three models use the same hyperparameters (<math id="S6.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.01</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S6.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{0}=0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{0}=0.3</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S6.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1.0</annotation></semantics></math>) without any retuning, demonstrating that GrMoE’s hyperparameters transfer across scales. The only change is the routing rank, which follows the <math id="S6.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}\approx d/N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}\approx d/N</annotation></semantics></math> heuristic (<math id="S6.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}=48" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>48</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}=48</annotation></semantics></math> at 350M, <math id="S6.SS3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>64</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64</annotation></semantics></math> at 1.3B, <math id="S6.SS3.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>64</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64</annotation></semantics></math> at 2.7B). This ease of scaling is a practical advantage over methods like Switch Transformer, where the load balancing loss weight and capacity factor often require retuning at each scale.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17798v1/fig3_training_dynamics.svg" id="S6.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/134;" width="476" height="134"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S6.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Training dynamics comparison. GrMoE produces stable, balanced routing throughout training at both scales.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.4 </span>Analysis and Ablations</h3>

<section id="S6.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">6.4.1 </span>Token-Level Routing Analysis</h4>

<div id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To move beyond aggregate statistics, we analyze what the learned routing actually captures. We sample 10K tokens from the OpenWebText validation set and categorize them into six types: punctuation, function words, common nouns, proper nouns, numbers/math tokens, and code tokens (identified by the presence of programming syntax). For each MoE layer of the 1.3B model, we record the top-1 expert assignment and the routing entropy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The results reveal clear specialization patterns (Figure <a href="#S6.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 6.4.1 Token-Level Routing Analysis ‣ 6.4 Analysis and Ablations ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). Two experts consistently receive high-<math id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> values (<math id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa&gt;3.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>3.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa&gt;3.0</annotation></semantics></math>) and specialize sharply: one handles 78% of code tokens and 65% of math tokens, while the other captures 71% of proper nouns. The remaining experts have moderate <math id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> values (<math id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.0</annotation></semantics></math>) and handle broader categories. Function words and punctuation are routed with high entropy (mean <math id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H&gt;1.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1.8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H&gt;1.8</annotation></semantics></math>), indicating that these tokens are genuinely ambiguous and do not strongly belong to any single expert. This is exactly the behavior we want: the amortization network learns to express low confidence on linguistically ambiguous tokens and high confidence on specialized ones.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We further examine whether the amortization network’s value increases with the number of experts. On the 350M model with <math id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=8</annotation></semantics></math>, amortization improves PPL by 0.2 (18.3 <math id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\to</annotation></semantics></math> 18.1). On the 1.3B model with <math id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=16</annotation></semantics></math>, the improvement is 0.3 (14.1 <math id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\to</annotation></semantics></math> 13.8), suggesting that the benefit of per-token concentration scaling grows with the number of experts, as there are more routing decisions where token-level confidence matters. This addresses the question of when amortization is worth the added complexity: at <math id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N\geq 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N\geq 16</annotation></semantics></math>, the gains are meaningful and justify the 0.5% parameter overhead.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17798v1/fig4_token_routing.png" id="S6.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/180;" width="476" height="180" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S6.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Token-level routing analysis on the 1.3B model reveals interpretable expert specialization that correlates with learned concentration values.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS4.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">

<div id="S6.SS4.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS4.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S6.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 6.4.2 Post-Hoc Sparsity Tuning ‣ 6.4 Analysis and Ablations ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> demonstrates a key practical advantage. A model trained at <math id="S6.SS4.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1</annotation></semantics></math> can be deployed at <math id="S6.SS4.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=2</annotation></semantics></math> (effective 1.8 experts, 24% throughput gain) with only 0.2 PPL degradation, outperforming a separately trained Top-1 model (19.0 vs. 19.8 PPL). This eliminates the need to train separate models for different compute budgets (Figure <a href="#S6.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 6.4.2 Post-Hoc Sparsity Tuning ‣ 6.4 Analysis and Ablations ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). On the 1.3B model, the same pattern holds: <math id="S6.SS4.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=2</annotation></semantics></math> yields PPL 14.1 (vs. 13.8 at <math id="S6.SS4.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1</annotation></semantics></math>) with 1.21<math id="S6.SS4.SSS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> throughput, while a retrained Top-1 achieves PPL 15.1.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17798v1/fig5_pareto.svg" id="S6.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/328;" width="476" height="328"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S6.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Pareto frontier of PPL vs. throughput. A single GrMoE model (varying <math id="S6.F4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>) traces a smooth frontier that dominates separately trained softmax top-<math id="S6.F4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> models at every operating point.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS4.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">6.4.3 </span>Further Ablations</h4>

<div id="S6.SS4.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS4.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Removing <math id="S6.SS4.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{subspace}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>subspace</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{subspace}}</annotation></semantics></math> increases the collapse rate from 0% to 20% on the 350M model and from 0% to 25% on the 1.3B model, and worsens CV from .074 to .168 and .081 to .195 respectively. This confirms that geometric regularization is essential and not redundant with the Bingham gating mechanism (Table <a href="#S6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 6.4.3 Further Ablations ‣ 6.4 Analysis and Ablations ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
</div>

Mean over 5 seeds.</span></figcaption>
