<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(20)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text">where we utilize the fact that <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\geq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\geq 1</annotation></semantics></math>. Because <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{k}^{(\alpha)}\leq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>G</mi><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{k}^{(\alpha)}\leq 1</annotation></semantics></math>, we can conservatively bound the ratio’s left side directly: <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-G_{k}^{(\alpha)}\leq G_{k}^{(\alpha)}(N-k)\exp(-\alpha\delta_{k}(x))\leq(N-k)\exp(-\alpha\delta_{k}(x))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>G</mi><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>G</mi><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-G_{k}^{(\alpha)}\leq G_{k}^{(\alpha)}(N-k)\exp(-\alpha\delta_{k}(x))\leq(N-k)\exp(-\alpha\delta_{k}(x))</annotation></semantics></math>.
Rearranging this inequality logically establishes <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{k}^{(\alpha)}\geq 1-(N-k)\exp(-\alpha\delta_{k}(x))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>G</mi><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{k}^{(\alpha)}\geq 1-(N-k)\exp(-\alpha\delta_{k}(x))</annotation></semantics></math>.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Proof of Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2 (Collapse Resistance via Subspace Separation). ‣ 4 Theoretical Analysis: Concentration and Sparsity ‣ Grassmannian Mixture-of-Experts:Concentration-Controlled Routing on Subspace Manifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a></h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">Let the unscaled logit be mapped as <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\kappa}_{e}=\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>κ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\kappa}_{e}=\kappa_{e}\|P_{e}x\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. By the stated assumptions, inputs are drawn from a balanced uniform mixture over expert-specialized target distributions: <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\sim\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{D}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\sim\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{D}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For an input sampled securely from the target distribution (<math id="A1.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\sim\mathcal{D}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\sim\mathcal{D}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>), the target concentrated logit holds strongly <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\kappa}_{i}\geq\kappa_{\min}\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>κ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\kappa}_{i}\geq\kappa_{\min}\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>. Simultaneously, for any distinct non-target expert <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j\neq i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j\neq i</annotation></semantics></math>, the geometric bounded overlap strictly limits <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|P_{j}x\|^{2}\leq\rho\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|P_{j}x\|^{2}\leq\rho\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>, verifying <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\kappa}_{j}\leq\kappa_{\max}\rho\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>κ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\kappa}_{j}\leq\kappa_{\max}\rho\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>.
The separation gap isolating the target expert from competitors is therefore robustly lower bounded: <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\kappa}_{i}-\tilde{\kappa}_{j}\geq\gamma(\kappa_{\min}-\rho\kappa_{\max})\equiv\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>κ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>κ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≡</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\kappa}_{i}-\tilde{\kappa}_{j}\geq\gamma(\kappa_{\min}-\rho\kappa_{\max})\equiv\Delta</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">The routing probability securing the target expert is limited natively via:</span></p>
<table id="A1.E21" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E21.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{i}^{(\alpha)}(x)=\frac{1}{1+\sum_{j\neq i}\exp(-\alpha(\tilde{\kappa}_{i}-\tilde{\kappa}_{j}))}\geq\frac{1}{1+(N-1)\exp(-\alpha\Delta)}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo rspace="0.055em">+</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>κ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>κ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>≥</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{i}^{(\alpha)}(x)=\frac{1}{1+\sum_{j\neq i}\exp(-\alpha(\tilde{\kappa}_{i}-\tilde{\kappa}_{j}))}\geq\frac{1}{1+(N-1)\exp(-\alpha\Delta)}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(21)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text">Let <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=(N-1)\exp(-\alpha\Delta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=(N-1)\exp(-\alpha\Delta)</annotation></semantics></math>. Because <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/(1+\epsilon)\geq 1-\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/(1+\epsilon)\geq 1-\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, we confirm <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{i}^{(\alpha)}(x)\geq 1-\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{i}^{(\alpha)}(x)\geq 1-\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>.
Conversely, for an input <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> drawn organically from an entirely disjoint non-target distribution (<math id="A1.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\sim\mathcal{D}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\sim\mathcal{D}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j\neq i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j\neq i</annotation></semantics></math>), the probability of misrouting to <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> is identically capped:</span></p>
<table id="A1.E22" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E22.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{i}^{(\alpha)}(x)=\frac{\exp(\alpha\tilde{\kappa}_{i})}{\sum_{k=1}^{N}\exp(\alpha\tilde{\kappa}_{k})}\leq\frac{\exp(\alpha\tilde{\kappa}_{i})}{\exp(\alpha\tilde{\kappa}_{j})}\leq\exp(-\alpha\Delta)=\frac{\epsilon}{N-1}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>κ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>κ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>≤</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>κ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>κ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>ϵ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{i}^{(\alpha)}(x)=\frac{\exp(\alpha\tilde{\kappa}_{i})}{\sum_{k=1}^{N}\exp(\alpha\tilde{\kappa}_{k})}\leq\frac{\exp(\alpha\tilde{\kappa}_{i})}{\exp(\alpha\tilde{\kappa}_{j})}\leq\exp(-\alpha\Delta)=\frac{\epsilon}{N-1}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(22)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">The cumulative expected load over the entire space for expert <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> is evaluated as <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{g}_{i}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{j}}[g_{i}^{(\alpha)}(x)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{g}_{i}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{j}}[g_{i}^{(\alpha)}(x)]</annotation></semantics></math>. Injecting the bounded extremes yields:</span></p>
<table id="A1.E23" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E23.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1-\epsilon}{N}\leq\bar{g}_{i}\leq\frac{1}{N}(1)+\frac{N-1}{N}\left(\frac{\epsilon}{N-1}\right)=\frac{1+\epsilon}{N}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo>≤</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mi>ϵ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1-\epsilon}{N}\leq\bar{g}_{i}\leq\frac{1}{N}(1)+\frac{N-1}{N}\left(\frac{\epsilon}{N-1}\right)=\frac{1+\epsilon}{N}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(23)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p3.2.1" class="ltx_text">Given exactly <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bar{g}_{i}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bar{g}_{i}=1</annotation></semantics></math>, the true mean expected load is exactly <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/N</annotation></semantics></math>. The corresponding variance of this expected load across all experts assesses firmly as:</span></p>
<table id="A1.E24" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E24.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Var}(\bar{g})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\bar{g}_{i}-\frac{1}{N}\right)^{2}\leq\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\frac{\epsilon}{N}\right)^{2}=\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{N^{2}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>Var</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>ϵ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Var}(\bar{g})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\bar{g}_{i}-\frac{1}{N}\right)^{2}\leq\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\frac{\epsilon}{N}\right)^{2}=\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{N^{2}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(24)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS3.p3.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p3.3.1" class="ltx_text">Finally, substituting the global standard deviation <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\bar{g})}\leq\epsilon/N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>Var</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\bar{g})}\leq\epsilon/N</annotation></semantics></math> into the coefficient of variation safely returns:</span></p>
<table id="A1.E25" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E25.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{CV}(\bar{g})=\frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\bar{g})}}{1/N}\leq\epsilon=(N-1)\exp\!\big(-\alpha\gamma(\kappa_{\min}-\rho\kappa_{\max})\big)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>CV</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msqrt><mrow><mi>Var</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>≤</mo><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{CV}(\bar{g})=\frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\bar{g})}}{1/N}\leq\epsilon=(N-1)\exp\!\big(-\alpha\gamma(\kappa_{\min}-\rho\kappa_{\max})\big).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(25)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Bingham Normalizing Constant Approximation</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The normalizing constant <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z(\Lambda)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z(\Lambda)</annotation></semantics></math> of the Matrix Bingham distribution does not have a closed form. We use the saddle point approximation of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kume and Wood [2005]</a></cite>:</p>
<table id="A2.E26" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E26.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="Z(\Lambda)\approx(2\pi)^{d/2}|\Lambda^{*}|^{-1/2}\exp\!\big(\mathrm{tr}(\Lambda(\Lambda^{*})^{-1})\big)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≈</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><msup><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mpadded style="width:1.370em;" width="1.370em"><mi>exp</mi></mpadded><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mi>tr</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z(\Lambda)\approx(2\pi)^{d/2}|\Lambda^{*}|^{-1/2}\exp\!\big(\mathrm{tr}(\Lambda(\Lambda^{*})^{-1})\big)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(26)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is the solution to a system of implicit equations. For the gradient computation during training, we use automatic differentiation through the saddle point approximation, which is accurate to <math id="A2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(d^{-2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(d^{-2})</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="A2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\geq 32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\geq 32</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Extended Experimental Details</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The 350M model consists of 12 Transformer blocks with <math id="A3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{model}}=768" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>model</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>768</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{model}}=768</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{ffn}}=3072" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>ffn</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3072</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{ffn}}=3072</annotation></semantics></math>, and 12 attention heads. MoE layers replace the FFN in even-numbered blocks (6 MoE layers total). Each expert is a standard two-layer FFN with <math id="A3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{ffn}}/2=1536" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>ffn</mtext></msub><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1536</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{ffn}}/2=1536</annotation></semantics></math> hidden units, so the total parameter count per MoE layer matches a dense model with <math id="A3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{ffn}}=3072" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>ffn</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3072</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{ffn}}=3072</annotation></semantics></math> when 2 experts are active.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The 1.3B model consists of 24 Transformer blocks with <math id="A3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{model}}=2048" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>model</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2048</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{model}}=2048</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{ffn}}=5504" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>ffn</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5504</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{ffn}}=5504</annotation></semantics></math>, and 16 attention heads. MoE layers replace the FFN in even-numbered blocks (12 MoE layers total). Each expert has <math id="A3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{ffn}}/2=2752" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>ffn</mtext></msub><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2752</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{ffn}}/2=2752</annotation></semantics></math> hidden units with 16 experts per layer. The total active parameter count per forward pass (with 2 experts active) is approximately 1.3B, matching a dense model of equivalent size.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Both models use a learning rate of <math id="A3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> with cosine decay and 2000 warmup steps. The context length is 1024 tokens with the GPT-2 tokenizer (50257 tokens). The subspace regularization weight is <math id="A3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.01</annotation></semantics></math> with overlap threshold <math id="A3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{0}=0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{0}=0.3</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We found <math id="A3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> to be robust across a range of values: <math id="A3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\in\{0.005,0.01,0.02\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0.005</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.01</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.02</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\in\{0.005,0.01,0.02\}</annotation></semantics></math> all achieve 0% collapse on the 350M model, with PPL varying by less than 0.1. The overlap threshold <math id="A3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{0}=0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{0}=0.3</annotation></semantics></math> was chosen based on the observation that random subspaces in <math id="A3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{768}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>768</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{768}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="A3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}=48" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>48</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}=48</annotation></semantics></math> have expected overlap <math id="A3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}^{2}/d\approx 3.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>/</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>3.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}^{2}/d\approx 3.0</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math id="A3.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{0}=0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{0}=0.3</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to requiring overlap to be at most 10% of the random baseline. On the 1.3B model, we use the same <math id="A3.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.01</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A3.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{0}=0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{0}=0.3</annotation></semantics></math> without retuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Sampled-Pairs Approximation</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The full subspace overlap regularization <math id="A4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{subspace}}=\sum_{e\neq e^{\prime}}\max(0,\|U_{e}^{\top}U_{e^{\prime}}\|_{F}^{2}-\rho_{0}k_{r})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>subspace</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>≠</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{subspace}}=\sum_{e\neq e^{\prime}}\max(0,\|U_{e}^{\top}U_{e^{\prime}}\|_{F}^{2}-\rho_{0}k_{r})</annotation></semantics></math> requires computing <math id="A4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\binom{N}{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\binom{N}{2}</annotation></semantics></math> pairwise overlaps. For <math id="A4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=8</annotation></semantics></math> this is 28 pairs (negligible), but for <math id="A4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=64</annotation></semantics></math> it would be 2016 pairs. We approximate by sampling <math id="A4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> random pairs per training step and computing the regularizer only over those pairs. On the 350M model with <math id="A4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=8</annotation></semantics></math>, we compare <math id="A4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\in\{8,16,28\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>28</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\in\{8,16,28\}</annotation></semantics></math> (where 28 is the full computation). The results are indistinguishable: CV of .074, .074, .073 respectively, all with 0% collapse. On the 1.3B model with <math id="A4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=16</annotation></semantics></math>, we use <math id="A4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=64</annotation></semantics></math> (vs. 120 full pairs) and observe CV .081 vs. .079, confirming that the approximation is effective. We recommend <math id="A4.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=4N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=4N</annotation></semantics></math> as a default that provides sufficient coverage while keeping the cost linear in <math id="A4.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Pareto Frontier: PPL vs. Throughput</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The post-hoc sparsity tuning capability of GrMoE enables a single trained model to trace out a Pareto frontier of PPL vs. throughput by varying <math id="A5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> at inference time. On the 350M model, the frontier spans from (PPL 18.4, throughput 0.82<math id="A5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>) at <math id="A5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.5</annotation></semantics></math> to (PPL 19.0, throughput 1.41<math id="A5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>) at <math id="A5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=5.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=5.0</annotation></semantics></math>, with the default operating point at (PPL 18.1, throughput 1.0<math id="A5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>). By contrast, achieving a comparable frontier with softmax top-<math id="A5.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> routing requires training separate models for each <math id="A5.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> value, each taking the full training budget. The GrMoE frontier strictly dominates the softmax frontier at every throughput level: at matched throughput, GrMoE achieves 0.5–0.8 lower PPL than the corresponding retrained softmax model.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">On the 1.3B model, the Pareto frontier is even more favorable. At <math id="A5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=2</annotation></semantics></math>, GrMoE achieves PPL 14.1 with 1.21<math id="A5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> throughput, while a retrained Softmax Top-1 achieves PPL 15.1 at 1.35<math id="A5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> throughput. The 1.0 PPL gap at comparable throughput represents a significant quality improvement that would normally require substantially more compute to achieve through scaling.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Sensitivity to Initialization</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We examine whether the initialization of expert subspace frames <math id="A6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> affects the final routing quality. We compare three initialization strategies: random Haar initialization (our default), PCA initialization (initializing <math id="A6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> from the top-<math id="A6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> principal components of a random subset of training data, with different subsets for each expert), and identity-based initialization (initializing each <math id="A6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> as a contiguous block of columns from the identity matrix). On the 350M model, all three initializations converge to similar PPL (18.1, 18.0, 18.2 respectively) and CV (.074, .071, .078), with 0% collapse in all cases. The subspace regularization and Riemannian optimization are sufficiently powerful to overcome initialization differences, making GrMoE robust to this choice. We use random Haar initialization as the default for simplicity.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Comparison with Soft MoE</h2>

<div id="A7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Soft MoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Puigcerver et al., 2024</a>]</cite> replaces discrete token-to-expert assignment with a soft mixing mechanism where each expert receives a weighted combination of all tokens. This eliminates the discrete top-<math id="A7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> selection that causes training instability, but it does not provide the same benefits as GrMoE for three reasons. First, Soft MoE does not provide post-hoc sparsity control: the effective number of experts is determined during training and cannot be adjusted at inference time without retraining. Second, Soft MoE’s routing weights are computed via standard softmax over learned slot parameters, which provides no geometric structure or formal sparsity guarantees. Third, as our experiments show, Soft MoE still suffers from collapse in 8–15% of seeds, because the soft mixing does not prevent the underlying routing distribution from becoming degenerate.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">GrMoE and Soft MoE address different aspects of the MoE routing problem. Soft MoE addresses the discreteness of top-<math id="A7.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> selection by making the token-to-expert mapping continuous. GrMoE addresses the lack of geometric structure in the routing space by operating on the Grassmannian. In principle, the two approaches could be combined: one could use Grassmannian subspace affinities to compute the soft mixing weights in a Soft MoE framework, potentially inheriting the benefits of both. We leave this combination to future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A8" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix H </span>Downstream Task Evaluation</h2>

<div id="A8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While our primary evaluation uses perplexity on OpenWebText, we also evaluate the 350M GrMoE model on three downstream tasks via few-shot prompting: HellaSwag (commonsense reasoning), ARC-Easy (science questions), and PIQA (physical intuition). GrMoE achieves accuracy of 42.1%, 51.3%, and 65.8% respectively, compared to 41.5%, 50.8%, and 65.2% for Softmax Top-2 and 40.2%, 49.1%, and 64.0% for Switch. The improvements are modest but consistent, and they confirm that GrMoE’s perplexity advantage translates to downstream task performance. Expert Choice achieves 41.8%, 50.5%, and 65.0%, slightly below GrMoE despite comparable perplexity, suggesting that GrMoE’s more structured routing produces representations that are more useful for downstream reasoning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A9" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix I </span>Learned Concentration Values</h2>

<div id="A9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report the learned <math id="A9.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> values for each MoE layer of the 1.3B model after 150K training steps, averaged over 5 seeds.</p>
</div>
<div id="A9.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Layer 2 (earliest MoE): <math id="A9.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> values range from 0.8 to 1.5, with mean 1.1 and low variance across experts. This indicates that early layers have relatively uniform routing, consistent with the observation that early Transformer layers learn general features.</p>
</div>
<div id="A9.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Layer 6 (middle): <math id="A9.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> values range from 0.9 to 2.4, with mean 1.5. The variance across experts increases, indicating the beginning of specialization.</p>
</div>
<div id="A9.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Layer 12 (latest MoE): <math id="A9.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> values range from 0.4 to 4.2, with mean 2.1 and high variance. The expert with <math id="A9.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa=4.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa=4.2</annotation></semantics></math> is the code/math specialist identified in the token-level analysis. The expert with <math id="A9.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa=0.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa=0.4</annotation></semantics></math> is a generalist that handles function words and punctuation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A9.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The monotonic increase in mean <math id="A9.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> from early to late layers, and the increasing variance, are consistent with the hierarchical specialization pattern observed in dense Transformers. GrMoE discovers this pattern automatically through the learned concentration values.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A10" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix J </span>Reproducibility</h2>

<div id="A10.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A10.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All experiments use PyTorch 2.1 with CUDA 12.1. Random seeds are set for PyTorch, NumPy, and Python’s random module. The Riemannian Adam optimizer uses the same random seed as the standard Adam optimizer for fair comparison. Expert subspace frames are initialized from the Haar measure using QR decomposition of random Gaussian matrices. The GPT-2 tokenizer (50257 tokens) is used for all language model experiments. Training data is shuffled with a fixed seed for reproducibility. All reported results are averaged over 5 seeds with standard deviations reported in the tables.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A11" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix K </span>Token-Level Routing Details</h2>

<div id="A11.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A11.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Token categorization uses the following heuristics applied to the GPT-2 tokenizer vocabulary: punctuation tokens are identified by Unicode category; function words are drawn from a list of 150 English function words (determiners, prepositions, conjunctions, auxiliary verbs); code tokens are identified by the presence of programming syntax characters (braces, semicolons, indentation patterns, common keywords like <span id="A11.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">def</span>, <span id="A11.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">class</span>, <span id="A11.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">import</span>); number/math tokens contain digits or mathematical operators; proper nouns are identified by capitalization patterns in context; and common nouns are the remainder. This categorization is approximate but sufficient to reveal clear specialization patterns.</p>
</div>
<div id="A11.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A11.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The learned <math id="A11.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> values on the 1.3B model range from 0.4 (most generalist expert) to 4.2 (most specialized expert, handling code tokens). The correlation between <math id="A11.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> and the entropy of expert <math id="A11.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>’s token type distribution is <math id="A11.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=-0.87" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.87</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=-0.87</annotation></semantics></math> (Pearson), confirming that high-<math id="A11.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> experts are indeed more specialized. This provides a concrete, interpretable meaning for the concentration parameter: <math id="A11.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> measures how sharply expert <math id="A11.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math> specializes in a particular region of the input space.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A12" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix L </span>Convergence Analysis</h2>

<div id="A12.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare training loss curves for GrMoE and Softmax Top-2 across 5 seeds on the 350M model. GrMoE’s loss curves form a tight band with inter-seed standard deviation of 0.02 at step 100K, while Softmax Top-2 shows a wider band with standard deviation 0.05, and 2 out of 5 seeds exhibit a characteristic “collapse dip” around step 20K–40K where the loss temporarily increases as expert utilization becomes imbalanced. GrMoE shows no such dips, consistent with the 0% collapse rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="A12.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A12.p2.1" class="ltx_p">On the 1.3B model, the convergence advantage is more pronounced. Softmax Top-2 requires approximately 30K steps to recover from collapse events (when they occur), effectively wasting 20–30% of the training budget. GrMoE’s stable convergence means that every training step contributes to improving the model, which partly explains the PPL advantage (13.8 vs. 14.2) despite using the same total compute.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A13" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix M </span>Per-Layer Sparsity Analysis</h2>

<div id="A13.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A13.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We examine how the learned <math id="A13.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> values and routing entropy vary across layers in the 1.3B model. Early MoE layers (layers 2, 4) have lower average <math id="A13.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> (mean 1.2) and higher routing entropy (mean 1.65), indicating that early layers benefit from distributing computation across more experts. Late MoE layers (layers 10, 12) have higher average <math id="A13.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> (mean 2.1) and lower routing entropy (mean 1.15), indicating sharper specialization. This pattern is consistent with the observation in dense Transformers that early layers learn general features while late layers learn task-specific features. GrMoE discovers this pattern automatically through the learned concentration values, without any explicit curriculum or per-layer hyperparameter tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="A13.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A13.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This observation motivates the future direction of per-layer <math id="A13.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> tuning mentioned in the conclusion: deploying early layers at <math id="A13.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.8</annotation></semantics></math> and late layers at <math id="A13.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1.5</annotation></semantics></math> could potentially improve the PPL-throughput tradeoff beyond what uniform <math id="A13.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> achieves.</p>
</div>
</section>
</article>
</div>
